case: A 31-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of worsening pelvic pain that begins 1 to 2 days before each menstrual period, deep pain with intercourse, and inability to conceive after 18 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Her partner's semen analysis is normal. Pelvic examination shows a normal-sized, fixed, retroverted uterus, tender nodularity along the uterosacral ligaments, and a 6-cm left adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a 6-cm left ovarian cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes. At laparoscopy, the cyst contains thick dark brown fluid, red and blue-black implants cover the uterosacral ligaments and pelvic peritoneum, and dense adhesions bind the left ovary to the pelvic sidewall. Biopsy specimens show endometrial glands and stroma with hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Diagnosis: endometriosis with a left ovarian endometrioma.

questions.stem: Her implants are concentrated on the ovaries, the uterosacral ligaments, and the dependent pelvic peritoneum. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this distribution of her lesions?
options: Hematogenous spread of endometrial cells to distant organs and tissues
Metaplasia of the pleural and peritoneal mesothelium
Retrograde flow of menstrual tissue through the uterine tubes
Direct downgrowth of the basalis into the myometrium
approach: Note where the implants sit: ovaries and the lowest parts of the pelvic peritoneum.
Ask which theory delivers endometrial fragments into the pelvis and lets them settle by gravity.
Match that pattern to retrograde menstruation, and keep the other theories for unusual sites.
questions.why: Retrograde menstruation is the leading theory of endometriosis. During menses, fragments of viable endometrium pass backward through the uterine tubes, spill onto the ovaries, and settle in the dependent pelvis, where they implant and respond to ovarian hormones. That is why the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and pelvic floor peritoneum are the most common sites. The implants bleed with each cycle, which explains the chocolate cyst, the adhesions, the painful periods, the deep dyspareunia, and the infertility.
whyNot: Vascular or lymphatic spread is the best explanation for rare distant lesions, such as endometriosis in the lung or a distant scar. It does not explain clustering in the dependent pelvis.

Coelomic metaplasia is the favored theory for endometriosis in sites menstrual flow cannot reach, such as the pleura, or in women who have never menstruated. It does not explain a pelvic, gravity-dependent pattern.
Correct.
Growth of the basal endometrium down into the myometrium describes adenomyosis, which stays inside the uterine wall.

questions.stem: Her 46-year-old aunt has a 1-year history of heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding and severe cramping with each period. Pelvic examination shows a symmetrically enlarged, globular, soft, tender uterus about the size of a 12-week gestation, with smooth contours and no adnexal masses. A hysterectomy is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination of the uterus?
options: Endometrial glands and stroma deep within the myometrium
Well-circumscribed whorled nodules of smooth muscle in the wall
Endometrial implants on the uterine serosa only
Crowded endometrial glands with cytologic atypia
approach: Pick out the key exam finding: a uniformly enlarged, soft, tender uterus with smooth contours.
Link heavy bleeding and dysmenorrhea with a diffusely enlarged uterus to adenomyosis.
Predict the histology: endometrial glands and stroma inside the myometrium.
questions.why: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue, glands and stroma, lying within the myometrium. The ectopic tissue bleeds and provokes smooth muscle hypertrophy, so the whole uterus becomes enlarged, globular, boggy, and tender. Women in their 40s with heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea are the typical patients. Endometriosis places the same tissue outside the uterus, and a leiomyoma makes the uterus irregular and firm.
whyNot: Correct.
Leiomyomas are firm, discrete nodules of smooth muscle that make the uterus irregular and lumpy. They are usually not tender, and they would be the answer for a firm, nodular uterus.
Implants on the serosa are endometriosis. That condition causes pain and adhesions, but it does not enlarge the uterus symmetrically.
Crowded glands with atypia describe atypical endometrial hyperplasia. It causes abnormal bleeding, usually without a tender, enlarged uterus.

questions.stem: Two months later, she comes to the emergency department because of sudden severe lower abdominal pain while standing at work. Ultrasonography shows a collapsed left ovarian cyst and free fluid in the pelvis. In which of the following spaces has the fluid most likely collected?
options: Vesicouterine pouch
Hepatorenal recess
Left paracolic gutter
Rectouterine pouch
approach: Recognize rupture of the endometrioma, which spills old blood and cyst fluid into the peritoneal cavity.
Use her position: upright, so fluid runs to the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity.
Recall that in a standing woman this is the peritoneal recess between the uterus and rectum.
questions.why: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in a standing or sitting woman. It lies behind the uterus and in front of the rectum, so free blood, pus, or cyst fluid collects there first. It sits just above the posterior vaginal fornix, which is why fluid there can be seen on transvaginal ultrasonography and sampled through the posterior fornix. Endometriosis implants are also common on its peritoneum for the same gravity-dependent reason.
whyNot: The vesicouterine pouch lies between the bladder and the uterus. It is shallower and higher than the pouch behind the uterus.
The hepatorenal recess is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when a person lies supine. It is not the first collecting site in an upright patient.
The paracolic gutters carry fluid between the upper abdomen and the pelvis. They are channels, and fluid drains through them toward the pelvis.
Correct.

topics: Peritoneal recesses of the female pelvis

questions.stem: Her 16-year-old sister has crampy lower abdominal pain that begins with the onset of menstrual flow and lasts 1 to 2 days, with nausea. Her pelvic examination and pelvic ultrasonography are normal. Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains the sister's pain?
options: Cyclic bleeding from endometrial implants on the peritoneum
Prostaglandin-induced myometrial contraction and ischemia
Peritoneal irritation from a ruptured ovarian follicle
Swelling of endometrial tissue within the myometrium
approach: Note the timing: pain starts with menses in an adolescent with a normal pelvis.
Classify it as primary dysmenorrhea, which has no structural cause.
Recall the mediator: endometrial prostaglandins released as the endometrium sheds.
questions.why: Primary dysmenorrhea is menstrual pain without pelvic disease. When progesterone falls at the end of the cycle, the shedding endometrium releases prostaglandins, mainly PGF2-alpha. These cause strong, uncoordinated myometrial contractions that compress uterine vessels and make the muscle ischemic, which produces crampy pain. Prostaglandins also cause the nausea and loose stools that often go with it, and NSAIDs relieve it by blocking prostaglandin synthesis.
whyNot: Bleeding implants cause secondary dysmenorrhea from endometriosis, which is the explanation for this patient's own pain. Her sister has a normal examination and no sign of structural disease.
Correct.
A ruptured follicle causes mittelschmerz, which is one-sided pain at midcycle around ovulation. It does not start with menstrual flow.
Endometrial tissue within the myometrium is adenomyosis. It causes secondary dysmenorrhea in older women with an enlarged, tender uterus.

dx: Acute endometritis after cesarean delivery complicated by placenta accreta
case: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, undergoes repeat cesarean delivery at 39 weeks' gestation after an unsuccessful trial of labor with membranes ruptured for 18 hours. She has had two previous cesarean deliveries. The placenta is implanted on the anterior lower uterine segment over the prior incision and does not separate; it is removed piecemeal by manual extraction, with blood loss of 1400 mL. Pathologic examination shows chorionic villi attached directly to myometrial smooth muscle. On postoperative day 2, her temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. The uterine fundus is markedly tender, and the lochia is foul smelling. Diagnosis: acute endometritis after cesarean delivery complicated by placenta accreta.

questions.stem: She improves with intravenous antibiotics. Five months later, she has persistent intermenstrual spotting and dull pelvic ache. An endometrial biopsy is obtained. Which of the following findings would best establish a diagnosis of chronic endometritis?
options: Neutrophils within the lumens of endometrial glands
Plasma cells scattered in the endometrial stroma
Lymphoid aggregates in the basal endometrium
Decidualized stroma with hemosiderin deposits
approach: Separate the two forms: acute endometritis follows delivery or retained products and shows neutrophils.
Recall the cell that defines chronic endometritis because it is absent from normal endometrium.
Exclude findings that also occur in a normal cycle or after a recent pregnancy.
questions.why: Plasma cells are the diagnostic marker of chronic endometritis because the normal endometrium does not contain them. Chronic endometritis follows retained products of conception, prior pelvic infection, or an intrauterine device, and it causes irregular bleeding, pelvic pain, and infertility. Acute endometritis, like her postpartum infection, is a polymicrobial ascending infection with neutrophils, fever, and a tender uterus.
whyNot: Neutrophils in glands fit acute endometritis, and they also appear normally in menstrual endometrium. They do not establish a chronic process.
Correct.
Small lymphoid aggregates are a normal finding in the basal endometrium, so they do not define chronic inflammation.
Decidualized stroma reflects progesterone effect in pregnancy, and hemosiderin marks old bleeding. Neither defines chronic endometritis.

questions.stem: Blood cultures obtained on postoperative day 2 grow gram-positive cocci in chains. On blood agar, the colonies show a narrow zone of complete hemolysis. The isolate is resistant to bacitracin and enhances the hemolysis of Staphylococcus aureus in a CAMP test. Which of the following organisms is most likely?
options: Enterococcus faecalis
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus agalactiae
approach: Gram-positive cocci in chains point to streptococci or enterococci.
Complete (beta) hemolysis narrows it to group A or group B streptococci.
Bacitracin resistance and a positive CAMP test identify group B.
questions.why: Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus) is a beta-hemolytic streptococcus that is bacitracin resistant and CAMP positive. It colonizes the vagina and rectum of many women and causes postpartum endometritis and bacteremia, especially after prolonged rupture of membranes. In the newborn it is a leading cause of early-onset sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis, which is why pregnant women are screened late in the third trimester.
whyNot: Enterococcus faecalis is usually nonhemolytic and is identified by growth in bile and 6.5% salt. It can take part in polymicrobial endometritis but does not fit these tests.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic and grows as lancet-shaped diplococci that are optochin sensitive.
Streptococcus pyogenes is beta-hemolytic but is bacitracin sensitive and CAMP negative. It would be the answer for a sensitive isolate.
Correct.

questions.stem: During her earlier trial of labor, contractions grew stronger and more frequent as the fetal head descended and stretched the cervix. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this progressive strengthening of contractions?
options: Cervical stretch increasing posterior pituitary oxytocin release
Cervical stretch increasing anterior pituitary prolactin release
Rising progesterone increasing myometrial gap junctions
Falling estrogen increasing myometrial oxytocin receptors
approach: Recognize a positive feedback loop: contraction causes stretch, and stretch causes more contraction.
Identify the afferent signal (cervical stretch) and the hormone it releases.
Recall that oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary and acts with prostaglandins on the myometrium.
questions.why: Labor is a positive feedback loop called the Ferguson reflex. Stretch of the cervix by the presenting part sends afferent signals to the hypothalamus, which increases oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin and the prostaglandins it promotes make the myometrium contract harder, which pushes the head further and stretches the cervix more. The loop continues until the baby is delivered and the stretch stops.
whyNot: Correct.
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production. It does not increase uterine contraction.
Progesterone keeps the myometrium quiet in pregnancy. Its effective withdrawal, together with rising estrogen, increases gap junctions near term.
Estrogen rises toward term and increases oxytocin receptors and gap junctions. A fall in estrogen would weaken contractions.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her placenta could not separate from the uterine wall at delivery?
options: Implantation of the placenta over the internal cervical os
Failure of trophoblast to remodel the maternal spiral arteries
Deficient decidua basalis at the site of the uterine scar
Overgrowth of syncytiotrophoblast secreting excess hCG
approach: Note the pathology: villi attached directly to myometrium, which defines placenta accreta.
Ask what normally sits between villi and myometrium and allows a clean separation.
Connect the prior cesarean scar to a missing or thin decidua basalis.
questions.why: The decidua basalis is the maternal layer under the placenta, and it forms the plane along which the placenta separates after delivery. Where the decidua is thin or absent, as over a cesarean scar, the villi attach directly to myometrium (accreta), invade into it (increta), or pass through it (percreta). Prior cesarean delivery and placenta previa are the major risk factors, and the risk rises with each cesarean. The result is a placenta that will not separate and severe postpartum hemorrhage.
whyNot: Implantation over the cervical os is placenta previa, which causes painless bleeding. Previa raises the risk of accreta but does not by itself prevent separation.
Failed spiral artery remodeling causes preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. It reflects too shallow an invasion rather than abnormal attachment.
Correct.
Excess syncytiotrophoblast with very high hCG fits a hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma. It does not explain a normal placenta stuck to myometrium.

dx: Pelvic inflammatory disease with salpingitis and a tubo-ovarian abscess
case: A 22-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of lower abdominal pain, fever, and vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period ended 10 days ago. She has had a new sexual partner for 2 months and uses condoms inconsistently. Her temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Speculum examination shows mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os. Bimanual examination shows cervical motion tenderness, bilateral adnexal tenderness, and a tender right adnexal mass. Urine hCG is negative. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm3 (4500 to 11,000). Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a dilated, fluid-filled right uterine tube and a 6-cm thick-walled multiloculated mass involving the right ovary. Diagnosis: pelvic inflammatory disease with salpingitis and a right tubo-ovarian abscess.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how infection most likely reached her uterine tubes?
options: Hematogenous seeding of the tubes by Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Lymphatic spread through the parametrium from a postpartum uterus
Direct extension from a ruptured, inflamed appendix
Ascent of cervical gonococci, chlamydiae, and vaginal flora
approach: Connect the cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness to infection that began in the cervix.
Recall that PID spreads upward along mucosal surfaces from cervix to endometrium to tubes.
Name the usual organisms: N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and polymicrobial vaginal flora.
questions.why: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection. Organisms that infect the endocervix, most often Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, travel up through the endometrial cavity to the tubal mucosa, often after menses when the cervical mucus barrier is weakest. Anaerobes and other vaginal flora join in, so established PID and abscesses are polymicrobial. Cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever, and purulent cervical discharge are the classic findings.
whyNot: Tuberculous salpingitis does come from blood-borne spread, but it is chronic and granulomatous, without purulent cervicitis. It would fit a woman from an endemic area with infertility and weight loss.
Lymphatic spread through the parametrium is the route of postpartum and postabortion infections. She has not been pregnant.
A ruptured appendix can involve the right adnexa, but it begins with periumbilical pain and does not cause mucopurulent cervicitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: She recovers with treatment. Three years later, she comes to the emergency department because of vaginal spotting and right lower quadrant pain after 7 weeks of amenorrhea. Serum hCG is elevated, and ultrasonography shows an empty uterus and a gestational sac in the right ampulla. Which of the following best explains the link between her earlier infection and this pregnancy?
options: Antisperm antibodies that delayed fertilization in the tube
Scarring and loss of ciliated cells that slowed embryo transport
Persistent chlamydiae that attracted the embryo to the tubal wall
Luteal phase deficiency that prevented endometrial implantation
approach: Recognize a tubal ectopic pregnancy in a woman with prior salpingitis.
Recall what the host inflammatory response to chlamydial and gonococcal salpingitis does to the tube.
Link damaged cilia and partial obstruction to an embryo held in the tube.
questions.why: Salpingitis damages the tube mainly through the host inflammatory response. Neutrophils and cytokines destroy ciliated cells, and healing causes fibrosis, adhesions, and partial or complete blockage. Chlamydial infection is especially harmful because it is often silent and repeated, and the immune response to chlamydial antigens such as heat shock protein 60 drives the scarring. A partly blocked tube with poor ciliary transport lets sperm through but holds the larger embryo, so it implants in the tube. A fully blocked tube causes tubal infertility.
whyNot: Antisperm antibodies can reduce fertility, but they act before fertilization and do not cause an embryo to implant in the tube.
Correct.
Chlamydiae do not attract an embryo. The damage comes from scarring left by the immune response to infection.
A luteal phase defect impairs implantation in the uterus and causes early loss. It does not move implantation into the tube.

questions.stem: On the third hospital day, despite intravenous antibiotics, she suddenly has severe diffuse abdominal pain. Her temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse is 132/min, and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. The abdomen is rigid with diffuse rebound tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this change?
options: Rupture of a tubal ectopic pregnancy
Torsion of the right adnexa
Rupture of the tubo-ovarian abscess
Perihepatitis with liver capsule adhesions
approach: Note the sudden change from localized pelvic pain to diffuse peritonitis with shock.
Recall that a tubo-ovarian abscess can rupture and spill pus into the peritoneal cavity.
Exclude causes that do not fit a negative hCG or a septic picture.
questions.why: A tubo-ovarian abscess forms when an inflamed, pus-filled tube adheres to the ovary and the two form one walled-off cavity. If it ruptures, pus floods the peritoneal cavity and causes generalized peritonitis and septic shock, which is a surgical emergency. Women who survive often have adhesions and tubal damage that cause later infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain.
whyNot: Ectopic rupture causes hemorrhagic shock, but her urine hCG was negative, which rules it out.
Adnexal torsion causes sudden one-sided pain and vomiting. It does not cause diffuse peritonitis with high fever and septic shock.
Correct.
Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome) causes right upper quadrant pain from inflammation of the liver capsule. It does not cause sudden shock with a rigid abdomen.

questions.stem: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis infect columnar epithelial cells. In an adult woman, which of the following epithelia lines the vagina and explains why these organisms cause cervicitis rather than vaginitis?
options: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Ciliated and secretory simple columnar epithelium
Mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium
Transitional epithelium
approach: Recall the epithelium of each segment: tube, endometrium, endocervix, ectocervix, and vagina.
Note that the vagina and ectocervix share a thick squamous lining.
Connect the columnar endocervix to the site these organisms infect.
questions.why: The adult vagina and ectocervix are lined by thick nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which these organisms do not readily infect. The endocervix is lined by mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium, so the discharge of gonococcal and chlamydial infection comes from the cervical os. The uterine tube has ciliated simple columnar epithelium, which is why ascending infection damages it. The junction between the squamous and columnar zones is the transformation zone, where cervical dysplasia arises.
whyNot: Correct.
Ciliated simple columnar epithelium lines the uterine tube, which these organisms do infect in salpingitis.
Mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium lines the endocervix, the main site of gonococcal and chlamydial cervicitis.
Transitional epithelium lines the bladder and ureters. It is not found in the vagina.

dx: Preeclampsia with severe features and placental abruption
case: A 19-year-old primigravid woman at 34 weeks' gestation comes to the labor unit because of a severe headache and flashing lights in her vision since the previous evening. Her blood pressure at 20 weeks was 114/72 mm Hg. Today her temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 166/112 mm Hg; 15 minutes later it is 164/110 mm Hg. She has 2+ pitting edema of the legs and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Fundal height is 30 cm. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 1.1 (less than 0.3). Ultrasonography shows an estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile. One hour later, she has sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding; the uterus is firm and tender, and fetal heart tracing shows late decelerations. Diagnosis: preeclampsia with severe features complicated by placental abruption.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the maternal endothelial dysfunction that produced her hypertension and proteinuria?
options: Placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 binding VEGF
Placental hCG stimulating maternal thyrotropin receptors
Antiphospholipid antibodies activating maternal platelets
Excess endothelial nitric oxide relaxing systemic arterioles
approach: Start at the placenta: shallow trophoblast invasion leaves narrow, unremodeled spiral arteries.
Recall that the ischemic placenta releases antiangiogenic factors into the maternal blood.
Link loss of VEGF and placental growth factor signaling to leaky, constricted maternal vessels.
questions.why: In preeclampsia, trophoblast fails to remodel the maternal spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels. The underperfused placenta releases soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), a decoy receptor that binds VEGF and placental growth factor, and soluble endoglin, which blocks TGF-beta signaling. Without these signals the maternal endothelium makes less nitric oxide and prostacyclin, so vessels constrict, leak protein, and activate platelets. That endothelial injury explains the hypertension, proteinuria, cerebral symptoms, and liver and kidney damage.
whyNot: Correct.
Very high hCG can stimulate the TSH receptor and cause hyperthyroidism, as in a molar pregnancy. It does not cause endothelial dysfunction.
Antiphospholipid syndrome raises the risk of preeclampsia and thrombosis, but she has no history to suggest it, and it is not the general mechanism of the disease.
Nitric oxide production falls in preeclampsia. More nitric oxide would lower blood pressure.

questions.stem: Laboratory studies before delivery show: hemoglobin, 9.6 g/dL (11 to 14); platelet count, 78,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000); aspartate aminotransferase, 240 U/L (10 to 40); lactate dehydrogenase, 920 U/L (100 to 250). A peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following complications of her disorder do these findings indicate?
options: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
HELLP syndrome
Dilutional anemia of pregnancy
approach: Group the findings: hemolysis (schistocytes, high LDH), elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets.
Place them in context: a patient who already has preeclampsia with severe features.
Name the complication that combines all three.
questions.why: HELLP syndrome is hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, and it is a severe form of preeclampsia. Endothelial injury in small vessels shears red cells (schistocytes, high LDH), consumes platelets, and causes periportal hepatic necrosis that raises transaminases. Other complications of preeclampsia include eclamptic seizures, placental abruption, and fetal growth restriction, and she has two of these already. Delivery is the definitive treatment.
whyNot: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy causes liver failure with hypoglycemia, high bilirubin, and coagulopathy. Schistocytic hemolysis with low platelets in a preeclamptic woman fits HELLP better.
TTP also causes microangiopathic hemolysis and low platelets, but it is caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency and does not explain high transaminases in a woman with preeclampsia.
Correct.
Dilutional anemia is the normal mild fall in hemoglobin from plasma volume expansion. It does not cause schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, or liver injury.

questions.stem: Over the next 2 hours, she continues to bleed and develops oozing from intravenous sites. Which of the following sets of laboratory changes is most likely?
options: High fibrinogen, normal D-dimer, normal prothrombin time
Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged prothrombin time
Normal fibrinogen, normal D-dimer, prolonged bleeding time
Normal fibrinogen, high D-dimer, shortened prothrombin time
approach: Recognize the abruption: painful bleeding with a firm, tender uterus, unlike the painless bleeding of placenta previa.
Recall that the separating placenta releases tissue factor into the maternal circulation.
Predict consumptive coagulopathy: clotting factors and fibrinogen are used up while fibrin is broken down.
questions.why: Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally placed placenta, with painful bleeding and a tender, firm uterus. Hypertension, cocaine use, and abdominal trauma are its main risk factors. Damaged decidua and placenta release large amounts of tissue factor, which triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation. Fibrinogen and clotting factors are consumed, so the prothrombin time lengthens and fibrinogen falls, while breakdown of fibrin raises D-dimer. Placenta previa, by contrast, causes painless bright red bleeding and rarely causes DIC.
whyNot: High fibrinogen with normal clotting tests is the normal hypercoagulable state of late pregnancy. It does not explain oozing from intravenous sites.
Correct.
An isolated long bleeding time points to a platelet function defect. It does not explain consumptive bleeding after abruption.
A high D-dimer can occur with DIC, but consumption lengthens the prothrombin time rather than shortening it, and fibrinogen falls.

questions.stem: At her 28-week prenatal visit, before preeclampsia developed, which of the following sets of changes compared with her nonpregnant state would most likely have been present?
options: Cardiac output increased, vascular resistance increased, GFR decreased
Cardiac output decreased, vascular resistance decreased, GFR increased
Cardiac output unchanged, vascular resistance increased, GFR unchanged
Cardiac output increased, vascular resistance decreased, GFR increased
approach: Recall that normal pregnancy expands plasma volume and dilates systemic vessels.
Predict the effect on each variable: more volume and heart rate raise cardiac output, and vasodilation lowers resistance.
Apply the higher renal plasma flow to glomerular filtration.
questions.why: In normal pregnancy, progesterone, nitric oxide, and the low-resistance placental circulation lower systemic vascular resistance. Plasma volume and heart rate rise, so cardiac output increases by about 30 to 50 percent. Renal plasma flow and GFR rise by about 50 percent, so serum creatinine falls. Other normal changes include dilutional anemia, respiratory alkalosis from progesterone-driven breathing, and hypercoagulability. Preeclampsia reverses the vascular part of this picture with high resistance and vasoconstriction.
whyNot: High resistance and reduced GFR describe preeclampsia, not normal pregnancy.
Cardiac output rises in normal pregnancy. A falling output would suggest heart disease or severe volume loss.
Pregnancy changes all three variables. Unchanged output and GFR with high resistance fit none of its normal adaptations.
Correct.

dx: Candidal vaginitis in a pregnant woman with gestational diabetes
case: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of intense vulvar itching, burning with urination, and a white vaginal discharge. Gestational diabetes was diagnosed at 26 weeks, and her fasting glucose levels have been 105 to 120 mg/dL (target less than 95) on diet alone. She has taken no antibiotics. Pelvic examination shows erythematous, excoriated, edematous vulvar skin and a thick, white, curd-like discharge adherent to the vaginal walls. Vaginal pH is 4.2 (3.8 to 4.5). The whiff test is negative. A potassium hydroxide preparation confirms the diagnosis. Diagnosis: candidal vulvovaginitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient is at increased risk for her vaginal infection?
options: Loss of vaginal lactobacilli from recent antibiotic use
Neutropenia impairing phagocytosis of fungal elements
Increased vaginal glycogen and glucose available to yeast
Rise in vaginal pH that favors anaerobic bacterial overgrowth
approach: List her risk factors: pregnancy and poorly controlled gestational diabetes, with no antibiotic exposure.
Recall how high estrogen changes the vaginal epithelium and how hyperglycemia changes secretions.
Link more glycogen and glucose to better yeast growth and adherence.
questions.why: Candida albicans is part of normal vaginal flora and overgrows when local conditions favor it. High estrogen in pregnancy increases glycogen in the vaginal epithelium, and hyperglycemia adds glucose to vaginal secretions, so the yeast has more fuel and adheres better. Antibiotics that kill lactobacilli and impaired cell-mediated immunity are the other classic risk factors. The typical result is itching, a thick white curd-like discharge, a normal vaginal pH, and pseudohyphae on KOH preparation.
whyNot: Antibiotic use is a classic risk factor, but she has taken none.
Neutropenia predisposes to invasive fungal infection, but nothing suggests it here, and it is not the usual setting for vaginal candidiasis.
Correct.
A rise in pH with anaerobic overgrowth describes bacterial vaginosis. Her pH is normal, which fits candidiasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely on her potassium hydroxide preparation?
options: Motile pear-shaped organisms with flagella
Epithelial cells covered with adherent coccobacilli
Septate hyphae branching at acute angles
Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae
approach: Identify the organism from the clinical picture: curd-like discharge, itching, normal pH.
Recall why KOH is used: it dissolves epithelial cells and leaves fungal elements.
Pick the microscopic form of Candida albicans.
questions.why: Candida albicans is a dimorphic fungus. In tissue and on KOH preparation it appears as oval budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae, which are chains of elongated buds with constrictions at the joins. KOH dissolves epithelial cells and debris so these fungal elements stand out. A thick white discharge with intense itching and a normal pH fits this finding.
whyNot: Motile, flagellated pear-shaped protozoa on a saline wet mount identify Trichomonas vaginalis.
Epithelial cells studded with coccobacilli are clue cells, which identify bacterial vaginosis from Gardnerella vaginalis.
Septate hyphae branching at acute angles describe Aspergillus, which does not cause vaginitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three months after delivery, she returns because of a thin, gray, homogeneous vaginal discharge with a fishy odor that is worse after intercourse. She has no itching. Which of the following sets of findings would best distinguish this new condition from candidiasis and trichomoniasis?
options: pH above 4.5, positive whiff test, clue cells on wet mount
pH above 4.5, positive whiff test, motile flagellates on wet mount
pH 4.5 or lower, negative whiff test, pseudohyphae on KOH
pH 4.5 or lower, positive whiff test, abundant lactobacilli
approach: Recognize the clinical picture of bacterial vaginosis: thin gray discharge, fishy odor, little irritation.
Use pH to separate the infections: candidiasis keeps a normal pH, while BV and trichomoniasis raise it.
Separate BV from trichomoniasis by the wet mount: clue cells versus motile flagellates.
questions.why: Bacterial vaginosis is a shift from lactobacilli to Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes. With fewer lactobacilli, less lactic acid is made and the pH rises above 4.5. Anaerobes produce amines, which give a fishy odor when KOH is added (positive whiff test). The wet mount shows clue cells, epithelial cells coated with bacteria. Trichomoniasis also raises pH and can give a positive whiff test, so the wet mount is what separates the two. Candidiasis has a normal pH and a negative whiff test.
whyNot: Correct.
High pH, a positive whiff test, and motile flagellates fit trichomoniasis, which causes a frothy yellow-green discharge with irritation.
Normal pH, negative whiff test, and pseudohyphae describe candidiasis, which was her earlier infection.
Abundant lactobacilli keep the pH low and make a positive whiff test unlikely. This set describes no single infection.

questions.stem: Her glucose tolerance was normal at 12 weeks and abnormal at 26 weeks. Which of the following best explains why her glucose intolerance appeared in the second half of pregnancy?
options: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Placental lactogen increasing maternal insulin resistance
Placental insulin clearance lowering circulating insulin levels
Estrogen suppressing hepatic glycogen storage
approach: Note the timing: glucose intolerance appears as the placenta grows.
Recall which placental hormone rises with placental mass and opposes insulin action.
Link insulin resistance to gestational diabetes when beta cells cannot raise insulin output enough.
questions.why: Human placental lactogen (human chorionic somatomammotropin) rises with placental mass through the second and third trimesters. It acts like growth hormone, increasing maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis so more glucose and fatty acids reach the fetus. Progesterone, cortisol, and other placental hormones add to this effect. Most women raise insulin secretion to compensate; when beta cells cannot keep up, gestational diabetes develops, which is why screening is done at 24 to 28 weeks.
whyNot: Autoimmune beta cell destruction causes type 1 diabetes. Gestational diabetes is a state of insulin resistance with inadequate compensation.
Correct.
The placenta does break down some insulin, but most women respond by secreting more, and this does not explain the timing as well as rising placental lactogen.
This is not a recognized mechanism of gestational diabetes, and it would not explain insulin resistance that rises as the placenta grows.

dx: Chlamydial nongonococcal urethritis with reactive arthritis
case: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of a painful, swollen left knee and right ankle, pain in both heels, and red eyes. Three weeks ago, after unprotected intercourse with a new partner, he had burning with urination and a scant clear urethral discharge that he did not treat. His temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). Examination shows bilateral conjunctival injection, a warm left knee effusion, and tenderness at both Achilles tendon insertions. A Gram stain of urethral discharge shows many neutrophils and no organisms. Synovial fluid shows a leukocyte count of 18,000/mm3 (less than 200), no crystals, and a negative culture. A urine nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. HLA-B27 is positive. Diagnosis: chlamydial nongonococcal urethritis with reactive arthritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his joint disease?
options: Hematogenous seeding of the joints by viable urethral bacteria
Sterile immune-mediated synovitis triggered by infection
Monosodium urate crystal deposition provoked by fever
Autoantibodies against the Fc portion of IgG
approach: Note the sequence: urethritis, then arthritis, conjunctivitis, and enthesitis weeks later.
Use the sterile synovial fluid and HLA-B27 to place it among the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.
Choose an immune mechanism triggered by infection elsewhere.
questions.why: Reactive arthritis is a sterile, immune-mediated inflammation of joints, entheses, and eyes that follows a genitourinary or enteric infection. Nongonococcal urethritis is most often caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, followed by Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Trichomonas vaginalis. In people with HLA-B27, the immune response to bacterial antigens, which can persist in the synovium, drives inflammation of joints and entheses. The classic picture is arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis, with asymmetric large-joint arthritis and heel pain.
whyNot: Bacteria seeding the joint cause septic arthritis, as in disseminated gonococcal infection. His synovial culture is negative and his urethral Gram stain shows no gonococci.
Correct.
Gout comes from urate crystals, which are absent from his fluid, and it does not explain the conjunctivitis or urethritis.
Antibodies to the Fc portion of IgG are rheumatoid factor. Reactive arthritis is seronegative.

questions.stem: His partner is 24 weeks pregnant. Her cervical nucleic acid amplification test is positive for the same organism, but she has no symptoms. If she is not treated and delivers vaginally, her infant is at greatest risk for which of the following?
options: Conjunctivitis at 5 to 14 days, then afebrile pneumonia
Purulent conjunctivitis with corneal ulceration at 2 to 5 days
Early-onset sepsis with meningitis in the first days of life
Vesicles of the skin, eyes, and mouth in the first weeks
approach: Recognize that genital chlamydial infection is often silent in women.
Recall that the newborn acquires it in the birth canal and that it infects conjunctival and respiratory epithelium.
Match the timing: conjunctivitis in the first 2 weeks, then a staccato-cough pneumonia at 1 to 3 months.
questions.why: Most women with genital chlamydial infection have no symptoms, so it often goes untreated. An infant born through an infected cervix can develop inclusion conjunctivitis about 5 to 14 days after birth and an afebrile pneumonia with a staccato cough, often with eosinophilia, at 1 to 3 months. In adults the same organism causes urethritis, cervicitis, epididymitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and reactive arthritis. Testing and treating pregnant women prevents neonatal infection.
whyNot: Correct.
Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis at 2 to 5 days that can perforate the cornea is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.
Early-onset sepsis and meningitis are typical of group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Listeria.
Vesicles of the skin, eyes, and mouth are a form of neonatal herpes simplex infection.

topics: Chlamydial infection in women and newborns

questions.stem: The organism cannot be grown on cell-free culture media. Which of the following best describes the serovar and the form of the organism that was transmitted to him during intercourse?
options: Serovar A to C reticulate body
Serovar D to K reticulate body
Serovar A to C elementary body
Serovar D to K elementary body
approach: Match the disease to the serovar group: genital and neonatal infections are serovars D to K.
Recall the two forms in the chlamydial life cycle and which one survives outside cells.
Pick the small, metabolically inactive form that enters host cells.
questions.why: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium, so it cannot grow on cell-free media. It has two forms. The elementary body is small, metabolically inactive, and infectious, and it enters columnar cells by endocytosis. Inside a membrane-bound inclusion it converts to the reticulate body, which divides by binary fission and then converts back to elementary bodies that are released to infect new cells. Serovars D to K cause genital and neonatal infection, A to C cause trachoma, and L1 to L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum.
whyNot: Serovars A to C cause trachoma, an eye infection spread by hands and flies, and the reticulate body is the replicating intracellular form.
Serovars D to K fit his genital infection, but the reticulate body lives inside cells and does not transmit infection.
The elementary body is the infectious form, but serovars A to C cause trachoma rather than urethritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, he develops pain and swelling at the posterior aspect of the left testis, and the epididymis is tender and enlarged. Infection has spread backward from the urethra. Which of the following best describes the most likely route?
options: Prostatic urethra, seminal vesicle, efferent ductules, epididymis
Membranous urethra, ejaculatory duct, rete testis, epididymis
Prostatic urethra, ejaculatory duct, ductus deferens, epididymis
Spongy urethra, bulbourethral gland, ductus deferens, epididymis
approach: Write out the forward path of sperm from the seminiferous tubules to the external meatus.
Reverse it from the urethra to the epididymis.
Check which option keeps every structure in the correct order and skips no step.
questions.why: Sperm travel from the seminiferous tubules to the rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, and ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra. The urethra then continues as the membranous and spongy urethra. Urethral organisms that ascend reach the epididymis by running this path backward: prostatic urethra, ejaculatory duct, ductus deferens, and the tail of the epididymis. In sexually active men under about 35, C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae are the main causes of epididymitis.
whyNot: The seminal vesicle joins the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, and the efferent ductules lie between the rete testis and the epididymis. This route skips the ductus deferens.
The ejaculatory duct opens into the prostatic urethra, not the membranous urethra, and the rete testis lies beyond the epididymis on the path.
Correct.
The bulbourethral glands drain into the spongy urethra but have no connection to the ductus deferens.

topics: Path of sperm through the male tract

dx: Gonococcal Bartholin gland abscess with mucopurulent cervicitis
case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of a painful swelling of the left labium that makes walking and sitting difficult. She also has had a yellow vaginal discharge and spotting after intercourse for 1 week. Her temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F). Examination shows a 4-cm tender, warm, fluctuant mass in the posterior left vulvar vestibule at the 4 o'clock position, with surrounding erythema. Speculum examination shows a friable cervix with yellow mucopurulent discharge from the endocervical canal. There is no cervical motion tenderness. Gram stain of fluid drained from the mass shows gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils. An endocervical nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Diagnosis: gonococcal Bartholin gland abscess with mucopurulent cervicitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the vulvar mass formed?
options: Cystic dilation of a mesonephric duct remnant in the lateral vagina
Obstruction of a paraurethral gland duct beside the urethral meatus
Herniation of the bladder through the anterior vaginal wall
Obstruction of the greater vestibular gland duct with infection
approach: Use the location: posterolateral vestibule at the 4 o'clock position.
Name the gland whose duct opens there: the greater vestibular (Bartholin) gland.
Explain the abscess: a blocked duct traps secretions, which then become infected.
questions.why: The Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands lie deep to the posterior labia, and their ducts open into the posterolateral vestibule at about the 4 and 8 o'clock positions. When a duct is blocked, mucus builds up and forms a cyst; if it becomes infected, it forms a painful abscess. Most abscesses are polymicrobial, from skin and vaginal flora, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes some of them, as it did here. These glands are active in reproductive-age women, so a new Bartholin mass after menopause raises concern for carcinoma.
whyNot: A mesonephric duct remnant forms a Gartner duct cyst in the lateral vaginal wall, inside the vagina rather than in the vestibule.
Paraurethral (Skene) glands open beside the urethral meatus in the anterior vestibule, not at the 4 o'clock position.
Bladder herniation is a cystocele, a soft anterior vaginal wall bulge that is not tender or fluctuant.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two years later, she is hospitalized because of fever, migratory joint pain, tenosynovitis of the right wrist, and a few hemorrhagic pustules on her fingers. Blood cultures grow the same organism. This is her third episode of disseminated infection with this organism. Which of the following immune defects is most likely?
options: Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor
Deficiency of NADPH oxidase in phagocytic cells
Deficiency of terminal complement components
Selective deficiency of serum IgA
approach: Recognize disseminated gonococcal infection: arthritis, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions.
Note that repeated systemic Neisseria infection points to a host defect.
Recall that Neisseria species are killed mainly by the membrane attack complex.
questions.why: Disseminated gonococcal infection causes fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and a few pustules on the extremities, and it can progress to septic arthritis. Neisseria species are cleared largely by complement-mediated lysis through the membrane attack complex, C5 to C9. People who lack a terminal complement component have repeated disseminated gonococcal and meningococcal infections. Other forms of gonorrhea include purulent urethritis with intracellular gram-negative diplococci, cervicitis, PID, and neonatal conjunctivitis.
whyNot: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema from excess bradykinin, without recurrent infection.
NADPH oxidase deficiency (chronic granulomatous disease) causes infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.
Correct.
Selective IgA deficiency causes sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, and many patients have no symptoms.

questions.stem: The organism is oxidase positive, ferments glucose but not maltose, and was isolated on Thayer-Martin agar. She has had gonorrhea before, yet her earlier infection did not protect her. Which of the following properties of the organism best explains this lack of lasting immunity?
options: Antigenic variation of its pilus proteins
Polysaccharide capsule that blocks phagocytosis
Protein A that binds the Fc portion of IgG
M protein that inhibits complement activation
approach: Identify Neisseria gonorrhoeae from the biochemical results and the selective medium.
Ask which virulence factor lets it escape antibodies made during a previous infection.
Pick the factor that keeps changing its surface antigens.
questions.why: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose but not maltose and is grown on Thayer-Martin agar. Its pili attach to columnar epithelium, and the bacterium constantly rearranges its pilin genes so the pili change their antigens. Antibodies from one infection do not recognize the next strain, so reinfection is common and no vaccine exists. Its other virulence factors are IgA protease, Opa proteins, and lipooligosaccharide.
whyNot: Correct.
Gonococci lack a polysaccharide capsule. Neisseria meningitidis has one, which is the target of meningococcal vaccines.
Protein A is a virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus.
M protein is a virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes.

questions.stem: Her roommate has postcoital spotting and a yellow mucopurulent endocervical discharge with a friable cervix. Her nucleic acid amplification test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae is negative. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of the roommate's cervicitis?
options: Trichomonas vaginalis
Chlamydia trachomatis
Herpes simplex virus type 2
Candida albicans
approach: Recognize mucopurulent cervicitis: purulent discharge from the endocervical canal and a friable cervix.
Recall the two main causes, which both infect columnar endocervical cells.
With gonorrhea excluded, choose the other main cause, and contrast the cervical pictures of the distractors.
questions.why: Mucopurulent cervicitis is caused mainly by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which both infect the columnar cells of the endocervix. With a negative gonococcal test, chlamydia is the most likely cause, and it is the more common of the two. Because coinfection is frequent, women with cervicitis are tested for both. Trichomoniasis gives a strawberry cervix with punctate hemorrhages, and HSV gives an ulcerated cervix.
whyNot: Trichomonas vaginalis can inflame the cervix, but its classic picture is a strawberry cervix with punctate hemorrhages and a frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge. It is a much less common cause of mucopus from the endocervical canal.
Correct.
Herpes simplex virus causes ulcerative, necrotic cervicitis, usually with painful vulvar vesicles and ulcers.
Candida albicans causes vulvovaginitis with a thick white discharge. It does not cause mucopurulent cervicitis.

case: A 5-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of persistent bloody nasal discharge and rash. He was born at term after no prenatal care. His mother recalls a painless genital sore during the second trimester that healed without treatment. His temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F). Examination shows profuse blood-tinged rhinorrhea, a copper-colored maculopapular rash with peeling on the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Radiographs of the long bones show periostitis and metaphyseal lucencies. The infant's rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer is 1:64, and the mother's is 1:16. Diagnosis: early congenital syphilis.

questions.stem: If he is not treated, which of the following findings is most likely to appear later in childhood?
options: Notched, peg-shaped upper central incisors
Cataracts with a patent ductus arteriosus
Hydrocephalus with diffuse intracranial calcifications
Microcephaly with periventricular calcifications
approach: Separate early congenital syphilis (first 2 years) from late congenital syphilis (after 2 years).
Recall that late findings come from scarring and abnormal growth of teeth, bone, and cartilage.
Pick the late syphilitic finding and exclude the signature findings of other TORCH infections.
questions.why: Early congenital syphilis appears in the first 2 years with snuffles, a rash that involves the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone lesions. Untreated children develop late findings from damage to developing teeth, bone, and cartilage. These include Hutchinson teeth (notched, peg-shaped upper central incisors), mulberry molars, saddle nose, saber shins, interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural deafness.
whyNot: Correct.
Cataracts with a patent ductus arteriosus and deafness are the classic triad of congenital rubella.
Hydrocephalus with diffuse calcifications and chorioretinitis is the classic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis.
Microcephaly with periventricular calcifications is classic for congenital cytomegalovirus infection.

questions.stem: The mother is treated with penicillin. One year later, her RPR is nonreactive. Which of the following results is expected on her fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test, and why?
options: Nonreactive, because treponemal antibodies clear after treatment
Reactive, because anticardiolipin antibodies persist after treatment
Nonreactive, because the test detects only IgM antibodies
Reactive, because treponemal antibodies usually persist for life
approach: Separate the two test types: nontreponemal (RPR, VDRL) and treponemal (FTA-ABS).
Recall what each measures: antibodies to cardiolipin versus antibodies to treponemal antigens.
Predict the effect of treatment: RPR titers fall, while treponemal tests usually stay positive.
questions.why: Nontreponemal tests (RPR and VDRL) measure antibodies that react with cardiolipin. Their titers track disease activity and fall after treatment, often to nonreactive, so they are used to screen and to follow treatment. They can be falsely positive in pregnancy, SLE, and viral infections. Treponemal tests such as FTA-ABS detect antibodies to the organism itself and usually remain reactive for life, so they confirm infection but cannot show whether it was treated.
whyNot: Treponemal antibodies usually persist after successful treatment, so the FTA-ABS stays reactive.
Anticardiolipin antibodies are what the RPR measures, and her RPR is now nonreactive. FTA-ABS detects treponemal antibodies.
FTA-ABS detects IgG as well as IgM. A reactive result in adults often reflects long-lasting IgG.
Correct.

questions.stem: Fluid from a moist skin lesion on the infant's sole is examined directly for the causative organism. Which of the following methods is most likely to show it?
options: Gram stain of the lesion fluid
Culture on Thayer-Martin agar
Dark-field microscopy of the fluid
Culture on blood and chocolate agar
approach: Identify the organism: Treponema pallidum.
Recall two key facts: it is too thin to see with ordinary stains, and it cannot be grown on standard media.
Pick the method that shows live spirochetes directly.
questions.why: Treponema pallidum is a thin, tightly coiled spirochete. It is too thin to be seen on a Gram stain and cannot be cultured on standard laboratory media. Dark-field microscopy of fluid from a moist lesion shows motile corkscrew organisms. It is transmitted sexually and across the placenta, which is how this infant was infected.
whyNot: T. pallidum is too thin to resolve with a Gram stain under ordinary light microscopy.
Thayer-Martin agar is used to culture Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Treponema pallidum does not grow on it.
Correct.
Treponema pallidum does not grow on blood or chocolate agar or on any standard medium.

questions.stem: The organism crossed from maternal blood in the intervillous space into the fetal circulation. Which of the following layers forms the outer surface of the chorionic villi in direct contact with that maternal blood?
options: Cytotrophoblast layer
Syncytiotrophoblast
Decidua basalis
Amniotic epithelium
approach: Recall how the placenta forms: fetal chorion frondosum plus maternal decidua basalis.
Picture a mature villus from outside in: syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, connective tissue, fetal capillaries.
Pick the layer bathed by maternal blood in the intervillous space.
questions.why: The fetal part of the placenta is the chorion frondosum, made of villi, and the maternal part is the decidua basalis. Each villus is covered by syncytiotrophoblast, a multinucleated layer that sits in maternal blood in the intervillous space and makes hCG. Under it lies cytotrophoblast, then connective tissue and fetal capillaries that drain into the single umbilical vein. Organisms that cross the placenta must pass this barrier to reach the fetus.
whyNot: Cytotrophoblast lies under the syncytiotrophoblast and thins out later in pregnancy. It is not the outer surface.
Correct.
The decidua basalis is the maternal part of the placenta. It forms the floor of the intervillous space.
The amnion lines the amniotic cavity on the fetal side and does not contact maternal blood.

case: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of painful genital sores and a 3-day history of painful swelling in his right groin. The sores began as tender papules 5 days after unprotected intercourse with a new partner. Examination shows two 1.5-cm deep ulcers on the coronal sulcus with ragged, undermined borders and soft edges. The bases are friable, bleed easily, and are covered by a gray-yellow exudate. The right inguinal lymph nodes are matted, tender, and fluctuant. Dark-field examination of ulcer fluid is negative, the RPR is nonreactive, and PCR of ulcer fluid is negative for herpes simplex virus. Gram stain of ulcer exudate shows gram-negative coccobacilli in parallel chains. Diagnosis: chancroid due to Haemophilus ducreyi.

questions.stem: Another man seen the same day has a single genital ulcer. Which of the following additional findings would favor primary syphilis rather than chancroid in that patient?
options: Ragged, undermined edges with a gray exudate
Tender inguinal nodes that suppurate and drain
Clustered painful ulcers that began as vesicles
Painless indurated ulcer with rubbery nodes
approach: List the features that separate genital ulcers: pain, induration, base, and lymph nodes.
Recall chancroid: painful soft ulcer with ragged edges and painful suppurating nodes.
Recall primary syphilis: painless, firm, clean-based ulcer with painless firm nodes.
questions.why: The primary chancre of syphilis is a painless ulcer with a firm, indurated border and a clean base, often with painless, rubbery inguinal nodes. Chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, is the opposite: a painful, soft ulcer with ragged, undermined edges and a gray exudate, followed by painful inguinal nodes that can suppurate and drain. Herpes forms clusters of vesicles that break into shallow painful ulcers.
whyNot: Ragged, undermined edges with a gray exudate describe chancroid.
Tender nodes that suppurate and drain describe chancroid buboes.
Clustered painful ulcers that start as vesicles describe genital herpes.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man who has sex with men had a small painless genital papule that healed within a week. Three weeks later, he has fever, painful fluctuant inguinal lymph nodes above and below the inguinal ligament, rectal pain, and bloody rectal discharge. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1 to L3
Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Haemophilus ducreyi
approach: Note the sequence: a brief painless lesion, then painful buboes and proctocolitis.
Recognize lymphogranuloma venereum, an invasive lymphatic infection.
Match it to the invasive Chlamydia trachomatis serovars.
questions.why: Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1 to L3, which invade lymphatic tissue rather than staying in the mucosa. A small painless papule or ulcer heals quickly and is often missed. Weeks later, painful inguinal nodes enlarge into buboes that can rupture, and nodes on both sides of the inguinal ligament make the groove sign. Receptive anal exposure can cause proctocolitis with rectal pain and bloody discharge.
whyNot: Correct.
Serovars D to K cause urethritis, cervicitis, and neonatal infection. They stay in the mucosa and do not cause buboes.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes skin abscesses and can cause suppurative lymphadenitis, but it does not follow a painless genital papule or cause proctocolitis.
Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, in which the genital ulcer is painful and persistent rather than small and quickly healed.

questions.stem: Because coinfection is common, he is retested 3 months later. He now has a generalized nonpruritic rash, and his RPR is reactive at a titer of 1:64. The FTA-ABS is reactive. He does not recall any new sore. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?
options: Granulomatous necrotic nodules of skin and bone
Dilation of the ascending aorta with aortic regurgitation
Moist, flat, gray plaques in the perianal area
Loss of vibration sense and proprioception in the legs
approach: Use the timing and the high RPR titer with a diffuse rash to place him in secondary syphilis.
Recall the other lesions of the secondary stage.
Exclude findings that belong to tertiary syphilis, which takes years to develop.
questions.why: Secondary syphilis begins weeks to a few months after the chancre, which is often painless and unnoticed. Spirochetes spread through the blood and cause a diffuse rash that often involves the palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata, moist, flat, gray plaques in warm, moist areas such as the perianal skin. Nontreponemal titers are highest in this stage. Untreated disease then enters latency, and years later tertiary syphilis can cause gummas, aortitis, and tabes dorsalis.
whyNot: Gummas are granulomatous necrotic lesions of tertiary syphilis that appear years after infection.
Ascending aortitis with aortic regurgitation is a tertiary finding caused by endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.
Correct.
Loss of vibration and position sense is tabes dorsalis, a tertiary form of neurosyphilis.

questions.stem: His enlarged nodes are in the superficial inguinal group, which drains the skin of the penis. A malignancy at which of the following sites would spread first to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes instead of to this group?
options: Skin of the scrotum
Testis
Skin of the penile shaft
Perianal skin below the pectinate line
approach: Recall which structures drain to the superficial inguinal nodes: skin of the perineum, scrotum, penis, and lower anal canal.
Recall that the gonads develop in the abdomen and keep their lymphatic drainage there.
Pick the gonad, whose lymph follows the testicular vessels to the para-aortic nodes.
questions.why: Lymph follows the blood supply. The testis develops near the kidneys and descends, bringing its testicular artery, veins, and lymphatics from the abdomen, so testicular tumors spread first to the para-aortic nodes. The scrotal skin, penile skin, and perianal skin below the pectinate line drain to the superficial inguinal nodes. The same rule applies in women: the ovary drains to para-aortic nodes, and the vulva and distal vagina drain to superficial inguinal nodes.
whyNot: Scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, so scrotal cancer spreads to the groin.
Correct.
Penile shaft skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
Perianal skin below the pectinate line drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

topics: Lymphatic drainage of the pelvis and perineum

dx: Primary genital herpes (HSV-2) late in pregnancy
case: A 23-year-old primigravid woman at 37 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of painful genital sores, burning with urination, headache, and malaise. Her temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Examination shows multiple clusters of vesicles and shallow, painful ulcers on erythematous bases on the labia majora and minora, and bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. PCR of fluid from a vesicle is positive for herpes simplex virus type 2. Serum IgG antibodies to herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 are not detected. Diagnosis: primary genital herpes simplex virus type 2 infection late in pregnancy.

questions.stem: Scrapings from the base of a fresh vesicle are stained and examined. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Squamous cells with perinuclear halos and wrinkled nuclei
Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions
Histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic bacteria
Keratinocytes with large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions
approach: Recognize genital herpes: painful grouped vesicles that ulcerate, with fever and malaise in a primary infection.
Recall how herpesviruses change infected epithelial cells.
Pick the cytologic finding of a Tzanck smear.
questions.why: Herpes simplex virus causes infected keratinocytes to fuse into multinucleated giant cells, and the nuclei show ground-glass chromatin and intranuclear inclusions. A Tzanck smear of a vesicle base shows these cells, though PCR is now the preferred test. Primary infection causes many grouped vesicles that ulcerate, with fever, malaise, and tender nodes. The virus then becomes latent in sacral ganglia and can reactivate to cause milder recurrences. A newborn is usually infected during delivery.
whyNot: Squamous cells with perinuclear halos and wrinkled nuclei are koilocytes, the sign of human papillomavirus infection.
Correct.
Bacteria inside histiocytes (Donovan bodies) are the sign of granuloma inguinale from Klebsiella granulomatis.
Large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in keratinocytes are molluscum bodies of molluscum contagiosum.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the virus causing her infection?
options: Enveloped dsDNA virus latent in sacral sensory ganglia
Nonenveloped dsDNA virus persisting in basal keratinocytes
Enveloped dsDNA virus latent in trigeminal ganglia
Enveloped ssRNA retrovirus integrated in CD4 T cells
approach: Identify the virus from the PCR result: HSV-2.
Recall its structure: an enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus.
Recall where genital HSV hides between outbreaks and contrast it with HPV.
questions.why: Herpes simplex virus type 2 is an enveloped, double-stranded DNA herpesvirus. After the primary genital infection, it travels up sensory nerves and stays latent in the sacral dorsal root ganglia, then reactivates and travels back down to cause recurrent lesions. Human papillomavirus is a nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus that persists in basal keratinocytes. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause genital warts, and high-risk types 16 and 18 cause cervical and anogenital cancers.
whyNot: Correct.
A nonenveloped dsDNA virus in basal keratinocytes describes human papillomavirus.
Latency in the trigeminal ganglia is typical of HSV-1 after oral infection, not of genital HSV-2.
An enveloped ssRNA retrovirus that integrates in CD4 T cells describes HIV.

questions.stem: Three years later, she delivers her second child vaginally, with no herpetic lesions present, and receives a transvaginal pudendal nerve block for perineal anesthesia. Toward which of the following palpable landmarks is the needle directed?
options: Sacral promontory
Ischial tuberosity
Ischial spine
Pubic tubercle
approach: Recall the origin of the pudendal nerve: ventral rami of S2 to S4.
Trace its path: out the greater sciatic foramen, around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, then into the lesser sciatic foramen.
Pick the point where it is closest to a bony landmark felt through the vagina.
questions.why: The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, curves around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen in the pudendal canal. The ischial spine can be felt through the lateral vaginal wall, so anesthetic is injected just medial and posterior to it. The block numbs most of the perineum, the lower vagina, and the posterior vulva.
whyNot: The sacral promontory is the upper edge of S1 at the pelvic inlet and is far from the pudendal nerve.
The ischial tuberosity lies below the point where the nerve curves around the spine. It is the landmark for the transperineal approach, not for a transvaginal block.
Correct.
The pubic tubercle is the attachment of the inguinal ligament and is used as a landmark for inguinal hernias.

questions.stem: Her obstetrician explains that an infant exposed at delivery is at much higher risk of neonatal herpes during this primary infection than during a recurrence in a woman infected long before pregnancy. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Lack of maternal HSV-specific IgM for transfer across the placenta
Lack of secretory IgA in colostrum at the time of delivery
Lack of maternal cytotoxic T cells crossing into the fetus
Lack of maternal HSV-specific IgG for FcRn-mediated transfer
approach: Note her serology: no HSV IgG, so she has not yet made a mature antibody response.
Recall that the only antibody class that crosses the placenta is IgG, carried by the neonatal Fc receptor.
Link the absence of transferred IgG to an unprotected newborn exposed to large amounts of virus.
questions.why: Newborns depend on maternal IgG, which the syncytiotrophoblast moves across the placenta using the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), mostly in the third trimester. A woman with long-standing HSV infection has HSV-specific IgG that protects her baby, and she sheds less virus during a recurrence. In a primary infection near term, she has not yet made IgG that can be transferred, and she sheds large amounts of virus, so the newborn is far more likely to be infected. IgM is too large to cross the placenta, and secretory IgA in breast milk protects mainly the infant's gut.
whyNot: IgM is a pentamer that cannot cross the placenta, so it never provides passive protection to the fetus.
Secretory IgA in colostrum protects the infant's gut mucosa after birth. It does not prevent infection acquired in the birth canal.
Maternal T cells do not cross the placenta to protect the fetus. Passive protection of the newborn is antibody based.
Correct.
